I adored this game. I remember trying it around when it first came out and getting overwhelmed by the UI, but I gave it a real shot this time and I'm so glad I did. There's a lot of stuff on the UI, but it's not nearly as complex as it looks and it doesn't take long to get familiar with it.

A lot of pretend-Internet games (not sure what else to call them) I've played before have really out-of-touch, hamfisted writing, but this one surprised me with how good the writing was. The characters felt like real people, and the 2016-ness of the writing felt nostalgic as opposed to painfully dated. And the story is so good. It's unpredictable without doing that thing a lot of lazy writers do where they throw in "twists" that make no sense. That's a tough balance to strike. I was constantly second-guessing myself, and when I figured something out or made educated guesses that turned out to be correct, it was so satisfying. This is one of those rare games I desperately wish I could play for the first time again.

There were a lot of times when I "made mistakes" or regretted choices I made and thought I'd screwed up my playthrough, but this game autosaves everything you do and doesn't let you load previous saves, so the perfectionist streak I tend to have this kind of game was foiled, and I'm so glad it was. 

Your voyeurism itch will be scratched, the decisions you make will be complex and have real weight, you'll probably mess up at times, then you might realize that what you thought was a mess-up was actually the right thing to do, and sometimes there will be no clear right thing to do at all. Play it.

Where to begin with Orwell? I imagine that a lot of the reviews are going to criticize Orwell for it's biggest problem, that being the game constantly holding your hand. Orwell makes it next to impossible to fail given that it will highlight every single important piece of information. That said, you can't just go through uploading every data chunk that you find and expect to properly complete the game. There will be some strategy to your behaviors in the game and you will discover numerous different outcomes based on the path you choose. Orwell is middle of the road for me as a detective game. I like the concept and I appreciate the spin on this time game. It seems uncommon that a game like this would have you working FOR big brother. Orwell has strong replay value to it, but the real question will be do you want to after you're done. You can certainly play the game serious, but I had a lot more fun being deliberately silly with it and doing things that I knew would have a poor outcome. The bottom line is that the fun factor will depend on you and your personality. I feel Orwell is one of those middle of the road games that is best purchased on sale. I wasn't enough of a fan to explore the sequel, however it wasn't a terrible experience and it is deserving of a thumbs up. Orwell is a 3/5 for me.

A simple yet effective game on Osmotic Studios' part, Orwell introduces the player to a world featuring all the thematic faculties of its namesakes' original novel. Through only a computer screen, the player views much this populated universe through such a small window in its beautiful geometric collage art style. In a nation that spies on its citizens in the name of public safety and security, the player must make choices that directly impact the narrative, potentially leading to the suspects' fates in questionable circumstances. With Orwell, truth becomes fickle and fact becomes fiction as information the player chooses to upload draws parallels towards that same old novel. Additionally, with the suspects' profiles altered however the player sees fit, this game brings about a fair amount of replay-ability as the fate of the Nation is revealed by the players handiwork.

My only critique is how easily the story is driven through click and dragging of information that immediately becomes visible once the player scrolls through it. This choice in development diminishes some of the challenge in finding the facts through all the media debris. While I understand the developers chose the feature to avoid breaking their game, I believe having to read the actual articles and having more conflicting data to choose from would have made this game more enthralling.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a thought-provoking game that successfully delves into the complex world of surveillance and privacy, raising numerous ethical questions and dilemmas. Its core premise, which involves taking on the role of a government operative monitoring citizens' digital lives, is both innovative and unsettling. It challenges players to balance national security with personal privacy, making every decision carry significant weight and moral ambiguity.

Gameplay Mechanics

The mechanics are straightforward, primarily revolving around reading through documents, chat logs, and social media posts to piece together clues about potential threats. While this simplicity makes the game accessible, it can also lead to a repetitive and tedious experience. The process of sifting through information often lacks variety, and the gameplay can become monotonous over time. Moreover, the game's interface, although intuitive, sometimes suffers from minor bugs that can force you to reload the Game. There are also some minor instances where progression is unclear, leaving players uncertain about their next steps.

Narrative and Storytelling

One of the strengths of Orwell lies in its narrative, which includes several compelling plot twists that keep the player engaged. The story explores themes of power, trust, and the consequences of unchecked surveillance, offering moments of genuine intrigue and suspense. However, despite these high points, the overall plot can feel somewhat bland and unremarkable by the conclusion. The characters, while initially interesting, sometimes lack depth, and the story does not always capitalize on its potential to deliver a truly memorable experience.

Ethical Themes and Impact

Where Orwell truly shines is in its exploration of ethical issues. The game does not shy away from presenting the moral complexities of surveillance, forcing players to confront the impact of their actions on individuals' lives. This aspect of the game is its most compelling feature, prompting players to reflect on real-world implications and the delicate balance between security and privacy.

TLDR: 

Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a game with a powerful concept that effectively engages with important ethical themes. Its simple mechanics can become repetitive, and minor technical issues can hinder the experience. While the narrative has strong moments, it ultimately falls short of being truly remarkable. Nevertheless, the game’s exploration of surveillance and privacy makes it a worthwhile experience for those interested in thought-provoking and socially relevant games.

Pros:

- Engaging ethical themes and dilemmas
- Innovative and unsettling premise
- Compelling plot twists
- Intuitive interface

Cons:

- Repetitive and tedious mechanics
- Minor bugs and progression issues
- Overall bland and unremarkable plot
- Characters lack depth

[h2]Cons:[/h2]

Orwell asks the player a simple question: how far are you willing to go for security? This one question is carried throughout the entire game, including every decision you are asked to make and the few you make on your own, and it is up to the player to determine the answer to this question. Being allowed to peer more and more into the lives of the characters you are investigating gives both a feeling of doing something wrong and also how much I can get away with. My only major complaint with the gameplay is that, with a handful of exceptions towards the end of the game, the game highlights all the answers you need in blue without you needing to look for them or read anything besides these blue boxes. There will sometimes be false positives or conflicting information that you need to pick and choose what is "right," but besides this, the game never really challenges you. But Orwell never overstays it's welcome and is enjoyable from beginning to end.  (8/10)

Ayer terminé (bueno básicamente lo empecé y lo acabé terminando). Porque haciendo pausas y tal en unas 5 horas te lo terminas. 

Juego basado en la novela "1984" de George Orwell, dónde la gente intentaba rebelarse contra el gobierno y su intento de gobernar todo y a todos. 

El juego comienza que eres contratado para ser un investigador y que tienes que analizar información e ir recogiendo información de ciertas personas para ir rellenando una base de datos y poder tomar decisiones para el bien social. 

Nada más contratarte, hay un atentado en una de las ciudades (vaya casualidad), así que tienes que probar el sistema para buscar información de todo sospechoso que hubiera por la zona y poder así parar futuros atentados y castigar a los culpables. 

En principio suena bien, y la historia en general te mantiene entretenido. Pero no es un juego para todo el mundo. El juego consiste en mirar tu monitor como si estuvieras trabajando en algún sitio, en el que lo que haces es revisar artículos de periódico, los mensajes de otra gente, sus emails, sus FBs, fotos, etc. Poco a poco vas consiguiendo permisos para ir metiéndote más en las cosas privadas de los demás y poder revisar mejor que hacen. Pero básicamente lo que haces es mirar esos textos, y el juego mismo te indica si alguna parte de ese texto es importante para el caso en concreto.

Te marca un párrafo en azul porque hay un texto que comenta algo del atentado, o de la fecha indicada o de algo así. Te lo puede marcar en amarillo si hay unos datos contradictorios, por ejemplo si hay un post en FB que dice que tiene pareja y luego un mensaje por ahí que dice que es solter@. Aunque es un poco estúpido, porque si ves un mensaje del 2010 que dice que tiene pareja y uno de 2012 diciendo que es solter@ no es información incorrecta, ya que ha pasado un tiempo y esas cosas pasan. Pero bueno, el sistema detecta eso, y tu tienes eres el componente humano que le dice que esa información es valida o no, o cual de esos dos puntos mandar a la base de datos que estás creando. 

Según tus acciones, puedes investigar a unos u otros y recopilar información cada vez más precisa. Como digo, la historia es interesante, y es obviamente una crítica a los gobiernos que nos tienen cada día más controlados y que saben todo lo que hacemos y tecleamos en nuestros dispositivos. 

Pero (y es un pero muy grande) apenas se siente como un juego... a ver si entretiene, y eso es un gran punto a favor de cualquier juego. Pero dudo de que hubiera seguido "jugando" muchas más horas si no se hubiera solucionado el caso de una vez o si hubiera más casos parecidos después de acabar el primero. 

No es un juego que pueda recomendar, lo tengo, porque una vez fue gratis. Y para lo que me ha costado, he pasado una horas entretenido que ya es bastante más de lo que otros por los que sí he pagado pueden decir. Pero no puedo recomendarlo a la gente. Sí lo tienes de gratis, y un día te aburres, échale un ojo. 
Lo puedes poner en cualquier idioma, ya que solo es texto.

Orwell : Keeping an Eye on You shows and emphasizes well how much things taken out of their context can be manipulated to say anything and everything. In game, one run after the other, you will always have the very same elements, but you can reach diametrically different conclusions, which gives some replayability to the game (to get all achievements, you'll need at least 3 runs).

Since there is nearly no time pressure (apart from very specific moments), I indulged in reading everything the game had to offer and, following a guide to get all endings, I finished my first run in roughly 4h and subsequent ones in 2h or so.
Fortunately, the game has been translated in multiple languages because some characters mainly use abbreviations, which can make it difficult to understand to any non-native speaker.
Soundtracks do a great job and more than once, there will be these specific ones kicking in whenever you stumble upon a shocking/emotional revelation. And I must admit that some of them gave me the shivers.
This game's aesthetics are very much to my tastes. The low-poly designs are good-looking, and the uncluttered display makes Orwell easy to navigate.

Real-time discussions are interesting at first, and it makes our surveillance feel more fleshed out/real. But at the same time, it really breaks the rhythm and thus the immersion, especially on replay. Even at the highest speed, it is still unbelievably slow and you just can't skip these unsufferable parts. Though, mind that you can go back to specific chapters (it rewrites your progression) for achievement purposes and such. Moreover, once you've opened a real-time discussion, it will keep unraveling even if you don't stay to watch it til the end.
Should you want to be Orwell's E. Snowden, know that you'll need to do a piss-poor job from the very beginning. Yes, even before knowing that there is something wrong here, which makes no sense lore-wise.
